claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline is a single-phase FCC alloy.
Mn is an example of a high-cost constituent in this alloy.
Reducing one or more constituents of equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni can define quaternary or ternary derivatives.
Selective reduction or substitution of constituents decreases lattice distortion relative to the equiatomic quinary alloy.
Changing the composition of Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni-family alloys can alter their stacking-fault energy.
Lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion and therefore contributes to dislocation pinning or solid-solution strengthening.
A decrease in lattice distortion lowers dislocation pinning.
Stacking-fault energy governs whether FCC alloys deform primarily through dislocation slip, mechanical twinning, or strain-induced transformation.
The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy exhibits both dislocation slip and mechanical twinning during plastic deformation.
The equiatomic quinary baseline is predominantly twin-mediated rather than slip-mediated.
Constituent reduction shifts the dominant deformation mechanism from twin-assisted plasticity to dislocation slip.
Changes in twinning and dislocation activity alter strain hardening, strength, and ductility.
Cost-reduced quaternary and ternary derivatives will have lower room-temperature yield strength than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Cost-reduced quaternary and ternary derivatives will exhibit modified work-hardening behavior relative to the quinary baseline.
Cost-reduced quaternary and ternary derivatives will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the quinary baseline.
Cost-reduced derivatives will form fewer deformation twins than the equiatomic quinary baseline.
Mechanical-property variations across the alloy series will correlate with measured lattice distortion and deformation-twin density.
The proposed mechanism is limited to single-phase FCC alloys that remain phase-stable during identical processing and room-temperature quasi-static deformation.
Magnetic interactions and minor compositional variations may affect the magnitude of the strength and ductility changes.
Failure to observe systematic changes in lattice distortion, twin density, or mechanical properties relative to the controlled quinary baseline would falsify the proposed mechanism.
